title: False Positive Triage
summary: False positive triage is the review process that separates findings describing a real problem from findings describing the normal, expected behaviour of a system. In vulnerability management the same term covers scanner output that cannot be exploited in the deployed configuration, such as a library version flagged by a signature match when the vulnerable code path is never loaded or is unreachable from the network. Triage combines several signals: asset criticality, whether the component is reachable, whether a public exploit exists, and whether a compensating control already blocks the path. The mistake people make is treating a high false positive rate as a scanner defect to argue about rather than a measurable signal that should drive rule tuning, suppression with an expiry date, and documented evidence for auditors. Suppressing a finding without a written reason and a review date converts a noisy tool into a permanent blind spot.

beginner.definition: A false positive is a warning that turns out to be wrong. Triage is the work of checking each warning and deciding what it really means. You look at the alert, the system and the evidence, then choose a label. A false positive triage decision says the alert was a mistake, not a real problem.
beginner.whyItMatters: If you ignore a warning, you may miss a real attack. If you chase every warning, you have no time left for real work. Triage helps you spend your effort on the things that matter most. It also keeps trust in your tools, because people stop reading alerts they no longer believe. A clear triage habit turns a noisy queue into a short list you can act on.
howItWorks: A monitoring tool raises an alert and puts it in a queue for review.
An analyst opens the alert and reads the data that sits behind it.
They compare the alert with the normal activity recorded on that same system.
They check the asset owner, the software version and the network path.
If the alert was a mistake, they mark it false positive and write why.
The team then tunes the rule so the same mistake happens less often.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital night desk. A monitor beeps when a patient moves, so the nurse walks to the bed and looks. Most beeps are just a patient rolling over, and that is a false positive. The nurse still writes down each check, because one beep may be a real fall. If the nurse turned the monitor off, the ward would be quiet but unsafe. If the nurse answered every beep with a full emergency team, nobody would sleep and the staff would burn out. Good triage means a quick, honest look at each beep and a clear note about what was found.
takeaways: A false positive is a warning that turns out to be harmless in your environment.
Always write down why you closed an alert, so others can check the decision later.
Measure the false positive rate and improve the rule instead of blaming the analyst.

objectives: Explain what a false positive is and why every detection queue needs triage.
Describe the steps an analyst follows to check a single alert from start to finish.
Identify the common causes of false positives in scanners and monitoring tools.
Decide when a finding should be tuned, suppressed with an expiry date, or escalated.
Record triage decisions so that teammates and auditors can review the reasoning.
